newsitem.title: CHINA: China to attack leftism to push forward reform.
newsitem.headline: China to attack leftism to push forward reform.

text.p: A first draft of the address to be given by China's President Jiang Zemin at a key Communist Party congress next month contains an attack on hardline Marxists opposed to badly needed economic reforms, Chinese sources said.

The bid by the president and Communist Party chief to win support for new, sweeping reforms at the 15th party congress in late September or early October echoes the anti-leftist call by his late mentor and paramount leader Deng Xiaoping in 1992 that triggered China's current economic boom.
Western diplomats have voiced surprise at signals that Jiang has felt a need to confront hardliners, believed in recent years to be a spent force since reform ignited the economic boom.

"We must be on guard against rightism but priority should be given to vigilance against leftism at this juncture," a party source quoted Jiang's draft report as saying in a reference to Deng's long-held policy of maintaining a balance between more liberal reformers and Marxist extremists.

Jiang's battle cry is aimed at pushing ahead with unpalatable reforms that would reduce the role of the state sector in the economy and could force thousands of flagging and long-cosseted state enterprises toward bankruptcy.
The leftists are opposed to the state sector playing second fiddle to the non-state sector, espousing orthodox Marxist theory and opposed to many of Deng's market reforms.

Anti-leftism would be the flavour of the congress, Chinese sources said. "If we are to increase the intensity of reforms, we cannot not guard against leftism," said another source who asked not to be identified.

Vice-Premier and economic tsar Zhu Rongji, who has emerged as the strongest candidate to replace Li Peng as premier next year, is determined to reform state enterprises but only if the economy is stable and in order, the sources said.
He is in favour of slashing the number of employees of state firms enjoying cradle-to-grave welfare and boosting the efficiency of such enterprises, the sources said.
State firms still form the backbone of China's socialist system, although Beijing has tried gradually to reduce their role while allowing private and collective enterprises.
About 70 percent of China's 100,000 state firms are in the red and struggling to adapt since the country abandoned Soviet-style central planning and embraced market reforms almost two decades ago.
Reform of state enterprises is one of the thorniest ideological issues facing the leaders of a communist state in which assets are regarded as belonging to the proletariat.

China's leaders agree that tackling the lumbering state sector is among the most crucial reforms, but they have dragged their feet due to fears that bankruptcies would result in mass unemployment and social unrest.

Jiang, who is also chairman of the party's Central Military Commission, must use the congress to set his own stamp on party politics to win his stripes and endorse his position as Deng's heir, diplomats and Chinese analysts say.

The five-yearly party congress expected in late September or early October is to set the path of the world's most populous nation as it begins a new era without Deng or other veterans of the revolutionary generation of Mao Zedong.

Jiang's report would pay homage to Deng's slogan to build socialism with Chinese characteristics, the sources said, referring to Deng's fig-leaf phrase justifying such un-Marxist concepts as free markets, private enterprise and stock markets.
